# Energy supergradients and a globally positive affine base chart

This note proves the exact interface between the jointly concave
projective energy and the actual global supporting-cut construction.
It permits a source at the boundary of the base projection when the
ambient body is the canonical hull of finitely many full-dimensional
fibers. A simpler support argument obtains the positive chart directly,
without identifying an energy supergradient. No global payment or
simultaneous optimization of several source charts is asserted.

The energy theorem and equality classification are in
`candidate 5811f0ad1132ce56`.
The actual global-cut construction is in
`candidate 6748c967393345b9`.

## 1. Setup and exact statement

Let `P` be a finite nonempty subset of `R^n` and let each `K_p` be a
full-dimensional compact convex body in `R^d`, `d>=1`. Assume all
sampled anchored inclusions hold, and define the canonical hull

    C=conv(union_(p in P) {p} times K_p),  Q=conv(P).     (1)

In particular `C_p=K_p` at every sampled base. Completeness and integrality
of `P` are not needed for this ordinary geometric lemma. They may be
imposed when this construction is used for a mixed-integer family.
All base statements are relative to `aff(Q)` if the base rank is deficient.

For every `z in Q`, the fiber `C_z` is a convex body. On

    Omega_C={(z,x):z in Q, x in int(C_z)}

put `F(z,x)=E_(C_z)(x)^(1/d)`. Fix a sampled source `p in P` and
`y in int K_p`. Write `F_0=F(p,y)>0` and let `a_p` be its unique optimal
projective parameter. Then:

1. The continuous-coordinate derivative is

       grad_x F(p,y)=((d+1)/d) F_0 a_p.                 (2)

2. There exists a finite base vector `B` such that the global inequality

       F(z,x)<=F_0[1+B.(z-p)
                         +((d+1)/d)a_p.(x-y)]          (3)

   holds throughout `Omega_C`. Every supergradient of `F` at the source
   has the continuous component in (2).

3. Consequently the affine denominator

       L(z,x)=1+a_p.(x-y)+(d/(d+1))B.(z-p)              (4)

   satisfies `L>=1/(d+1)` on the ENTIRE compact body `C`, and
   `L>1/(d+1)` on `Omega_C`.

The boundary-base existence in part 2 is proved below using the finite
hull. For sources in the relative interior of the projection, ordinary
supergradient existence for a finite concave function already suffices.

## 2. Envelope derivative and the own-fiber denominator bound

For a fixed body `K`, the objective

    V(a,y)=int_K [1+a.(x-y)]^(-d-1) dx

is smooth in a neighborhood of every pair with a positive denominator
on compact `K`. At its minimizing parameter the `a`-Hessian is positive
definite. The implicit function theorem therefore continues the unique
stationary minimizer smoothly as `y` varies locally in `int K`; strict
convexity in `a` identifies it with the global minimizer. The envelope
derivative and escort normalization give

    grad_y E_K(y)
       =(d+1)a_p int_K L^(-d-2)
       =(d+1)E_K(y)a_p.

Taking the `d`th root proves (2). The sign is positive.

Concavity on the own fiber and its tangent plane imply, for `x in int K`,

    0<E_K(x)^(1/d)
      <=E_K(y)^(1/d)[1+((d+1)/d)a_p.(x-y)].             (5)

Thus the optimal source denominator is strictly greater than
`1/(d+1)` on `int K`, and by continuity it is at least `1/(d+1)` on
all of `K`. This uniform bound uses optimality; an arbitrary admissible
projective parameter need not have it.

## 3. Finite-hull fibers are uniformly Hausdorff-Lipschitz

For any unit continuous normal `u`, write `h_p=h_(K_p)(u)`. The exact
fiber support at a real base is the finite linear-programming value

    h_(C_z)(u)=max{sum_p lambda_p h_p:
                       lambda>=0, sum lambda=1,
                       sum lambda p=z}.                (6)

This follows directly from the convex-hull definition, including every
representation of `z`; maximizing the continuous support in each input
fiber is legitimate independently in the Minkowski sum.

Choose coordinates on the base affine hull, of rank `r`. The dual
polyhedron consists of affine functions `c+A.z` satisfying

    c+A.p>=h_p for all p in P.                          (7)

It is nonempty and pointed: a line in it would be an affine function
zero on every point of a full-affine-span set. Standard finite linear
programming duality gives an attained dual minimum at every `z in Q`.
An optimal face of a pointed polyhedron has a vertex. Each such vertex
is determined by `r+1` independent tight rows of the FIXED matrix with
rows `(1,p)`. Its coefficients are fixed linear functions of the selected
values `h_p`. There are finitely many possible independent row sets.

All fibers lie in a fixed continuous-coordinate ball, so `|h_p(u)|` is
bounded uniformly in `p,u`. Hence every dual vertex slope `A` has a
uniform bound `L_P`, independent of `u` and of which rows are active.
Formula (6) is the minimum of these admissible affine vertex functions.
It follows that

    |h_(C_z)(u)-h_(C_z')(u)|<=L_P |z-z'|,
    d_H(C_z,C_z')<=L_P |z-z'|.                          (8)

This proof includes projection boundary points. It uses the finite-hull
structure, not a presumed Lipschitz property of arbitrary convex slices.

The real fibers also have a uniform positive inradius. Choose balls of
one common radius inside the finitely many `K_p`. Any representation of
`z` places the corresponding weighted-center ball of the same radius
inside `C_z`. Near the fixed source `p`, (8) gives the stronger useful
fact that all nearby fibers contain a fixed ball about `y`.

## 4. Local Lipschitz energy and a finite boundary supergradient

Here are the needed regularity details, to avoid inferring a finite
boundary supergradient from concavity alone. In a sufficiently small
product neighborhood

    z in Q intersect B(p,epsilon),  x in B(y,epsilon),

all relevant fibers contain balls of a common radius `r>0` centered at
each marked point, and lie in a common bounded ball. Their minimizing
parameters have norm at most `1/r`, and by (5) their denominators are
at least `1/(d+1)` on their own bodies.

For two sufficiently close pairs `(K,x)` and `(K',x')` in this
neighborhood, a minimizing parameter for either pair remains admissible
for the other, with denominator at least `1/[2(d+1)]`. This follows by
matching points within Hausdorff distance and bounding the denominator
change by `(d_H(K,K')+|x-x'|)/r`.

The symmetric-difference volume is bounded by a constant times the
Hausdorff distance. For completeness, the bodies here contain a common
ball about `y`, so `K+delta B` lies in the dilation of `K` about `y` by
factor `1+delta/r_0`, for a uniform `r_0>0`. Apply this inclusion in
both directions and use uniformly bounded volumes. On the union of the
two bodies the tested inverse-power integrands and their derivatives
in the marked point are uniformly bounded. Testing the first minimizer
in the second objective and then reversing the roles therefore gives

    |E_K(x)-E_K'(x')|
       <=C[d_H(K,K')+|x-x'|].                           (9)

The energies have a uniform positive lower bound from their contained
marked balls and energy monotonicity. Taking the `d`th root preserves
this local Lipschitz estimate. Combined with (8), `F` is Lipschitz in
`(z,x)` on a small closed convex product neighborhood relative to `Q`.

To obtain the boundary supergradient explicitly from this fact, let
`f=-F` on that small closed convex neighborhood `D_0`, and let `L_0`
be a Lipschitz constant. Its infimal-convolution extension

    g(v)=inf_(w in D_0) [f(w)+L_0|v-w|]

is a finite convex function on the full vector space
`span(Q-Q) times R^d` and equals `f` on `D_0`. It therefore has a finite
subgradient at `(p,y)`. Negating that subgradient gives a local supporting
affine upper bound for `F`.

The local upper bound is global on `Omega_C`: given any other domain
point, a sufficiently short initial part of its segment from `(p,y)`
lies in `D_0`; compare the local support bound there with concavity along
the full segment. The continuous-coordinate component is forced by the
ordinary derivative (2), since both signs of every continuous-coordinate
variation are available at the source. Dividing its base component by
`F_0` defines the finite vector `B` in (3). A zero extension to the
orthogonal complement of the base affine span handles deficient rank.

Finally the bracket in (3) is positive throughout `Omega_C`. The identity

    L=1/(d+1)+(d/(d+1))
                  [1+B.(z-p)+((d+1)/d)a_p.(x-y)]

gives (4) and its strict interior-fiber bound. Approximating a boundary
point inside its own full-dimensional real fiber gives the closed-body
bound. No extension of energy to boundary marked points is needed.

## 5. Simpler direct positive-chart construction

If only a globally positive denominator is needed, part 3 admits a
shorter proof that does not require the base energy supergradient.
Choose a finite affine support majorant in direction `-a_p` touching
the sampled source:

    h_(K_z)(-a_p)<=h_(K_p)(-a_p)+b.(z-p)  for z in P.   (10)

Such a finite `b` exists by finite Farkas: any nonnegative infeasibility
certificate normalizes to an anchored representation of `p` violating
the actual support inclusion. If `a_p=0`, simply take `b=0`.
For every sampled fiber point,

    1+a_p.(x-y)+b.(z-p)
       >=1-a_p.y-h_(K_p)(-a_p)
       =min_(x in K_p)[1+a_p.(x-y)]>=1/(d+1).           (11)

Since the denominator is affine, this bound holds on the entire
canonical hull. It retains exactly the optimizing source denominator.
This `b` is not claimed to equal `dB/(d+1)` for an energy supergradient;
it solves a different, finite support-majorant problem.

In the global supporting-cut construction, the freely chosen affine
base denominator can consequently be set to this `b`, or to the vector
in (4). Choosing a tangent-continuation threshold strictly below
`1/(d+1)` then keeps the actual denominator on its pure inverse-power
branch everywhere in `C`, and in a small neighborhood of `C`. This is
an admissibility interface. It does not prove that this choice minimizes
continuation cost, pays a critical menu, or can be optimized independently
for several simultaneously constrained source charts.

## 6. Why the canonical hull qualification matters

For an arbitrary ambient convex body, a projection-boundary energy
supergradient need not be finite. Let

    C={(z,x):0<=z<=1, |x|<=1+sqrt(z)}.

Its radius is concave, so `C` is a compact convex body. At the center
of each round fiber,

    F(z,0)=|B_d|^(1/d)[1+sqrt(z)].

No finite affine upper support in the base direction touches at
`(0,0)`. Restricting to the minimal face and using only the finitely
many sampled base gaps does not repair this inward square-root growth.
For sampled bases `{0,1}`, the canonical fiber hull instead has radius
`1+z`, and the preceding theorem applies. In this example the direct
positive chart is still the constant one; the obstruction concerns
the stronger energy-supergradient assertion, not chart positivity.
